newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: France pushes in UN for Zaire force; U.S. hesitant.
newsitem.headline: France pushes in UN for Zaire force; U.S. hesitant.

text.p: France on Tuesday pushed for a Security Council resolution that would authorise intervention into eastern Zaire to protect refugees, but the United States and Britain appeared hesitant.
Diplomats said Germany and Italy were drafting a resolution but it did not contain a definitive call for intervention until further council discussions on Wednesday.

"There are a lot of questions and a lot of problems and not enough answers. So I think it is premature to discuss anything specific at this moment," U.S. Ambassador Madeleine Albright told reporters after closed-door consultations.
Britain's ambassador, Sir John Weston, confirmed "one delegation proposed that we should be thinking in terms of some kind of international presence to try to assure the security dimension."

This "would allow the humanitarian agencies to go about their business of feeding and providing and settling the refugees so that the refugees do not continue to stream off into the void in very large numbers and in great panic," Weston added.
But he said most members had not received instructions from their governments on how to proceed "and I don't know where we will come out at this stage."
French and British leaders intend to discuss the issue on Friday.
In Nairobi on Tuesday, African leaders urged the Security Council to deploy a "neutral force" in eastern Zaire to help 1.2 million Hutu refugees facing famine and epidemics.

After a four-hour summit in the Kenyan capital, seven east and central African leaders said the force should create safe corridors to repatriate the refugees to Rwanda and Burundi and provide temporary sanctuary for the huge mass of people.

The summit said bona fide refugees should be separated from "intimidators," the tens of thousands of former Rwandan government soldiers and militiamen mainly responsible for the genocide against minority Tutsis and moderate Hutus in 1994.

Some Security Council envoys said the future of the refugees was a key problem in considering humanitarian intervention. Many fear going back to Rwanda, where they do not expect justice. At the same time a new U.N. report made it clear that eastern Zaire was awash with arms destined for Hutu fighters who were running the refugee camps.
"The political context for humanitarian aid is not clear," one council diplomat said, referring to a possible reconstitution of the refugee camps.

In Marseille, a French spokesman said Paris was getting a favourable response to its proposal to send a multinational force to ensure security for the refugees. But so far only Spain, whose Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar was holding a bilateral summit with President Jacques Chirac in Marseille, has agreed to participate in the proposed force.
An Italian foreign ministry spokesman said there was no question at this stage of committing any European troops.
